newsitem.title: UK: Summary of events in UK election on Tuesday.
newsitem.headline: Summary of events in UK election on Tuesday.

text.p: Following is a summary of events on Tuesday in the British election campaign -
KNUTSFORD, England - A row over "sleaze" hijacks the campaign when former minister Neil Hamilton confronts Martin Bell who is trying to force him to stand down as a Conservative candidate.

The extraordinary row between Hamilton and Bell, a highly-respected BBC journalist, came as Bell was about to address an open-air press conference explaining why he was standing in the Tatton constituency of north-west England.
Hamilton's wife Christine asked Bell if he believed her husband was guilty of sleaze. "Do you accept a man is innocent until proved guilty?" she demanded. "Do you then accept my husband is innocent?"
LONDON - Britain's churches attack politicians for using tax cuts for the middle classes as a vote winner, and call for higher taxes to create new jobs and narrow the social divide.
"In the British election campaign, the political parties are competing for votes by promising low taxation," said a report produced for the Council of Churches for Britain and Ireland.
"When so many are living in poverty and unemployment, it is wrong to give priority to the claims of those who are already well off."
BIRMINGHAM, England - Prime Minister John Major makes an unashamed pitch for the votes of Britain's growing army of small businessmen by proposing a 800 million pound tax break for fledgling firms.
The plan is designed to overshadow the much-heralded launch due on Friday of the main Labour opposition party's small business manifesto.

The prime minister, whose party is running 20 points behind in the race for the May 1 election, was scathing about Opposition leader Tony Blair's claim that Labour had become the natural party of small business.
"I sometimes believe that this modern Labour party, if it had a collective grandmother, it would sell it," Major told a lunch for Asian small businessmen at Edgbaston cricket ground.

NEWLYN, England - Billionaire Sir James Goldsmith, creator of an anti-European party dedicated to protecting Britain's sovereignity, begins his election campaign by fishing for votes among disaffected trawlermen.

"You have been sold down the river, the industry has been destroyed and they want to destroy it further," he told a small crowd of supporters on the quayside at Newlyn, a fishing port in Cornwall at the south-western tip of England.

Around 100 yellow and red flags of Goldsmith's Referendum Party fluttered from the large fleet of trawlers at anchor in Newlyn, where fishermen say European Union rules governing the size of catches are slowly killing off their livelihoods.
